entry.title: Combined summary - Should wallets default to Taproot or SegWit receive addresses while some services still reject bc1p?
entry.summary: Address compatibility remains a significant challenge for users of cryptocurrency wallets, especially due to the varying address formats supported across different services. When attempting to withdraw funds from exchanges or other platforms to wallets such as Gem Wallet, users often face "invalid address" errors. These problems frequently occur when receiving addresses are generated in the Taproot (bc1p...) format, which, while valid according to Bitcoin's protocol standards, is not yet universally recognized by all sending entities. Wallet developers are confronted with important decisions regarding which default address format to provide for receiving transactions. The choice between Taproot (bc1p...) and SegWit (bc1q...) must weigh the advantages of adopting newer protocols against the necessity for broad compatibility. Some products opt for Taproot by default in an effort to promote adoption of its technical improvements, whereas others prefer SegWit, given its widespread acceptance among exchanges and related services. The decision-making process is typically informed by the level of support observed among major platforms as well as a commitment to ensuring a frictionless experience for end-users. When both Taproot and SegWit are available, presenting this choice to users requires careful user interface (UI) and user experience (UX) design. The selection mechanism should be easily discoverable for those encountering compatibility issues but should not introduce confusion or complexity for users unfamiliar with the underlying technical distinctions. Ensuring that alternative address formats are accessible without overwhelming the majority of users is critical for maintaining a streamlined user experience. Service-side support for advanced address types like bc1p remains inconsistent, and there is currently no definitive, comprehensive resource listing all services and exchanges that accept Taproot addresses. As a result, wallet teams and users often rely on trial and error to identify compatible platforms. This situation highlights the need for improved communication within the ecosystem and underscores the value of community-maintained resources such as the [Bech32 adoption database](https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Bech32_adoption) and [whentaproot.org](https://whentaproot.org/), which provide up-to-date information about service support for various address types. The debate over whether to default to Taproot or remain with SegWit reflects broader considerations around user needs and technological advancement. While some argue that Taproot’s benefits—such as lower transaction fees and enhanced privacy—are marginal for the average user, proponents emphasize that the core intention behind Taproot was to offer universal advantages. Taproot provides a unified output type that accommodates both key and script spending scenarios, reduces on-chain data exposure, and incentivizes privacy-enhancing practices by obscuring wallet policies unless revealed through more complex scripts. However, the privacy gains are limited until Taproot sees greater adoption, and the cost savings are less pronounced in periods of low network fees. Concerns about post-quantum (PQ) security have also been raised, but these are considered largely irrelevant in the context of address type selection, as public keys are inherently designed to be exposed. There is recognition that most users prioritize simplicity and reliability over potential privacy enhancements or minor fee reductions. For mainstream adoption, the presence of incompatible address types complicates the user experience, particularly when closed-source platforms lag in integrating new standards. While proposals for universal Bitcoin addresses capable of encoding arbitrary spending conditions exist, such approaches may introduce further risks and complexity. For wallet implementers, steering users toward unsupported address formats is impractical, as users are likely to switch applications rather than advocate for broader compatibility. The development of clear guidance, robust support resources, and intuitive interfaces is paramount to bridging the gap between protocol advancements and practical usability. Recent updates to product documentation reflect an increased effort to educate users about the differences between address types. For instance, Gem Wallet now includes explanations of both bc1q (SegWit) and bc1p (Taproot) addresses on its [support page](https://gemwallet.com/bitcoin-wallet/), along with a [guide](https://docs.gemwallet.com/blockchains/bitcoin/bitcoin-address-types-bc1q-and-bc1p) to assist users who encounter "invalid address" messages. Linking to resources like [whentaproot.org](https://whentaproot.org/) empowers support teams to direct users to current lists of compatible services, facilitating smoother experiences and greater transparency as the Bitcoin ecosystem continues to evolve.
